strengths: Addresses an important problem: improving reasoning-model calibration while retaining task accuracy. The proposed correctness-plus-Brier reward is simple and readily compatible with existing RL training.
The central Brier-score incentive argument is sound: for an answer with correctness probability p, expected reward is maximized at q=p, yielding p², which increases with correctness probability.

Experiments cover factual QA and mathematical reasoning, with multiple out-of-domain evaluations and useful classifier, probe, and token-probability baselines. HotpotQA results are particularly encouraging: ECE decreases from 0.370 to 0.030 while accuracy remains close to RLVR.
The test-time confidence aggregation experiments and detailed per-dataset results provide useful evidence beyond the headline calibration comparison.
weaknesses: Novelty and comparative evidence are insufficiently established. The paper acknowledges prior RL methods using proper scoring rules, including Brier rewards and self-reflective rationales, but does not compare directly against them. A calibration-only reward baseline is especially important to establish the practical benefit of adding correctness reward and substantiate the proposed failure mode of deliberately incorrect, zero-confidence answers.

The experiments do not isolate the reward's contribution from uncertainty reasoning, prompting, and additional computation. RLCR receives explicit uncertainty-analysis training, whereas RLVR confidence is elicited through a different appended prompt. Missing controls include RLCR without uncertainty analysis and RLVR with matched analysis prompts and generation budgets. Section 4.5 compares outputs from different generators, so it does not establish that reasoning causally improves confidence estimation.

Claims of preserving accuracy and outperforming calibration baselines are too broad. For math-trained models, OOD accuracy falls from 52.5% with RLVR to 50.9% with RLCR, and to 43.8% with SFT+RLCR. On CommonsenseQA, math-trained RLCR worsens ECE from 0.126 to 0.340. On SimpleQA, the HotpotQA-trained Brier classifier substantially outperforms RLCR in Brier score (0.112 versus 0.241). Aggregate averages obscure these important limitations.

The theoretical presentation requires substantial correction. Section 2 mixes minimized losses with maximized scores, and its spherical-score expression omits the outcome. Appendix A contains incorrect signs in the expected-score expansion and W(p), and incorrectly simplifies W'(p) to S(p,1)-S(p,0), rather than λ-S(p,1)+S(p,0). The main Brier result is recoverable, but the general argument also needs explicit regularity assumptions. Furthermore, incentive compatibility at an ideal optimum does not guarantee that finite-capacity, empirically trained models will be calibrated.

Experimental reproducibility and robustness are incomplete. Main results use one generator architecture and lack repeated-training variability or confidence intervals. Important details such as learning rates, training duration, classifier training-set construction, and checkpoint selection are missing. The blanket temperature-zero evaluation description leaves stochastic test-time sampling settings unclear. Llama-3.1-8B judging is used across several benchmarks without a reported validation of judge reliability.

The auxiliary interpretations overreach their evidence. Better calibration alone does not guarantee better candidate ranking or best-of-N accuracy. Likewise, sampled unique answers need not exhaust the answer space, so their confidences need not sum to one; confidence conditioned on different reasoning traces further complicates this interpretation. These analyses are suggestive, but do not establish the claimed general improvements in belief coherence.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: improving confidence calibration while retaining the accuracy gains of reinforcement learning. The proposed correctness-plus-Brier reward is simple and practically appealing.
The core Brier incentive claim is sound: expected reward equals p² − (q − p)², so unrestricted optimization favors truthful confidence and the most accurate answer.

HotpotQA results are promising: RLCR reduces ECE from 0.37 to 0.03 while retaining similar accuracy (62.1% versus 63.0%). Experiments cover factual QA, mathematics, distribution shifts, and several classifier and probe baselines.
Confidence-weighted voting and analysis ensembling demonstrate potential downstream uses of the learned confidence estimates.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution is insufficiently established against the closest prior work. Section 5 acknowledges existing RL methods using Brier and other proper-scoring rewards, but these are not evaluated directly. There is no controlled Brier-only versus correctness-plus-Brier comparison demonstrating the claimed avoidance of accuracy degradation.

The experiments do not isolate uncertainty reasoning. Section 4.5 compares classifiers consuming outputs from different generators, with different answer and reasoning distributions. Comparable aggregate accuracy does not remove this confound. A matched RLCR variant without analysis, and interventions removing or replacing analysis for fixed answers, are needed to support the central reasoning claim. RLVR also receives a different confidence-elicitation procedure.

Claims of calibration improvement without accuracy loss are too broad. In Table 1, math-trained RLCR has lower OOD accuracy than RLVR (50.9% versus 52.5%); SFT+RLCR falls to 43.8%. On in-domain mathematics, classifiers outperform ordinary RLCR in both AUROC (0.78 versus 0.67) and Brier score (0.15 versus 0.17). Dataset averages also hide reversals: HotpotQA-trained RLCR worsens CommonsenseQA ECE from 0.092 to 0.302, and its SimpleQA Brier score is substantially worse than the Brier classifier’s (0.241 versus 0.112).

The theoretical presentation needs substantial correction. Section 2 mixes loss-minimization and score-maximization conventions, and its spherical score omits dependence on the outcome. Appendix A contains sign errors in the expected-score expressions and an incorrect final derivative simplification. The Brier theorem remains readily repairable, but the broader proof assumes differentiability without stating the necessary restrictions. Moreover, an incentive result for unrestricted optimization does not guarantee calibration or preserved accuracy after finite, parameter-shared RL training.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility are incomplete. Main comparisons lack uncertainty estimates or repeated RL training runs, and only one generator backbone and size are tested. Important details such as learning rates, training duration, classifier training-data construction, and checkpoint selection are missing. The Llama-3.1-8B correctness judge is not validated against human labels, although its decisions directly determine calibration measurements.

The secondary analyses overinterpret their evidence. Confidence-weighted voting gains are small and lack uncertainty estimates or compute-matched comparisons against RLVR and classifier reranking. Section 4.6 treats confidence sums near one as desirable without establishing that the sampled answer set is exhaustive; its intra-solution analysis also lacks a baseline supporting the claimed reduction in variability.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of reasoning-model training with a simple, practical objective combining correctness and Brier rewards, without requiring a separate confidence model at inference.

Provides substantial empirical evidence of calibration improvements. On HotpotQA, ECE decreases from 0.37 to 0.03 while accuracy remains close to RLVR (62.1% versus 63.0%); average out-of-domain accuracy and calibration also improve.
Evaluates two training domains and multiple downstream benchmarks, including meaningful comparisons against full-model confidence classifiers, linear probes, and answer-token probabilities.

The central Brier-reward incentive result is valid: expected reward equals p² − (q − p)², encouraging truthful confidence and selection of the most likely correct answer under the theorem's assumptions.
Confidence-weighted voting and uncertainty-analysis ensembling demonstrate useful applications of the learned confidence estimates.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution over prior RL calibration methods is insufficiently isolated. The paper acknowledges previous Brier-reward training but provides neither direct comparisons nor calibration-only and reward-weight ablations to establish the practical benefit of adding correctness rewards.

The claim that uncertainty reasoning improves calibration lacks a controlled test. Section 4.5 compares classifiers trained on outputs from different generators, changing both solution distributions and analysis content. Comparable aggregate accuracy does not remove this confound. RLCR without uncertainty analysis and matched-output analysis-removal experiments are needed.

Claims of consistently superior calibration and preserved accuracy are stronger than the results. For math training, RLCR has worse in-domain AUROC/Brier than the classifiers (0.67/0.17 versus 0.78/0.15). On CommonsenseQA, its ECE worsens to 0.340 from RLVR's 0.126; GPQA accuracy falls from 50.0% to 43.3%. SFT+RLCR reduces average out-of-domain accuracy to 43.8%, versus 52.5% for RLVR.

The theoretical presentation contains substantive mathematical errors requiring correction. Section 2 mixes scoring-rule minimization and maximization, and its spherical-score expression omits the outcome. Appendix A has incorrect signs in the definitions and derivation of W; the correct derivative is λ − S(p,1) + S(p,0). The general argument also needs explicit regularity assumptions. The valid idealized Brier result does not guarantee calibrated finite-capacity models after RL optimization.

Experimental robustness and reproducibility are incomplete. Main generator results use only Qwen2.5-7B, with no reported variation across training seeds or uncertainty estimates for the main comparisons. Learning rates, training duration, classifier-training details, and sampling settings for test-time scaling are insufficiently specified. The Llama-3.1-8B correctness judge is not independently validated.

Some secondary interpretations are overstated. Sampled distinct answers need not exhaust the answer space, so their confidence sum need not equal one. Likewise, improved calibration alone does not guarantee better answer ranking or best-of-N accuracy. These analyses should distinguish calibration, discrimination, and coherence.

strengths: RLCR provides a simple, useful modification to reasoning-model training: combining correctness rewards with a proper scoring rule addresses the degenerate incentive to produce deliberately incorrect answers with zero confidence. The central Brier-score result is sound: after optimizing confidence, expected reward equals p² and therefore increases with correctness probability.

The empirical calibration improvements are substantial while average task accuracy remains competitive. On HotpotQA, ECE decreases from 0.37 to 0.03 with accuracy changing from 63.0% to 62.1%; on math, ECE decreases from 0.26 to 0.10 with nearly unchanged accuracy.

Evaluation extends beyond the main Qwen2.5 experiments to OLMo-2 and Qwen3, multiple out-of-domain benchmarks, expressive confidence classifiers, probes, and adapted RL-calibration baselines. Appendix I and the log-score experiments provide useful evidence supporting joint correctness-and-calibration training.

The paper includes dataset-level bootstrap intervals, confidence distributions, inference ablations, and test-time scaling experiments. These analyses show that confidence estimates contain useful discrimination information rather than merely collapsing to a constant.
weaknesses: The theoretical presentation needs correction and narrower claims. Appendix A gives inconsistent signs in the definitions and derivation of W; the correct derivative is λ − S(p,1) + S(p,0), not the final expression printed there. The general proof also assumes differentiability without stating it. Although the Brier result survives these corrections, incentive compatibility under ideal optimization does not establish that finite-capacity models trained with GRPO will become calibrated or preserve accuracy.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior RL-based confidence training using proper scoring rules. The meaningful advance is adding the correctness term and demonstrating its practical benefits for reasoning models; neither proper-score calibration nor confidence-weighted voting is itself new.

Out-of-domain gains are uneven, and broad superiority claims exceed the evidence. For the HotpotQA-trained model, CommonsenseQA ECE worsens from 0.09 with RLVR to 0.30 with RLCR, while the Brier classifier substantially outperforms RLCR on SimpleQA calibration. For math training, RLCR trails the classifiers in in-domain AUROC and Brier score, and GPQA accuracy falls from 50.0% to 43.3%. These tradeoffs deserve more prominence.

The uncertainty-reasoning ablation changes prompts only at inference, so it does not cleanly isolate the contribution of training with analysis. Appendix G additionally compares classifiers receiving outputs from different generators. A matched training ablation and interventions on analysis content would better establish whether the generated reasoning causally improves confidence estimation.

Reproducibility and statistical support remain incomplete. Classifier/probe training configurations and data construction are insufficiently specified, repeated RL training seeds are not reported, and bootstrap intervals capture evaluation-sample uncertainty rather than training variability. Test-time scaling lacks uncertainty intervals and compute-matched comparisons against classifier-based selection. Evaluation also relies on an unaudited 8B LLM judge for several benchmarks.

strengths: The method addresses an important practical problem with a simple, actionable change to reasoning-model training. Combining correctness and Brier rewards avoids the deliberately incorrect, zero-confidence solutions permitted by calibration-only rewards.

The main calibration gains are substantial while task accuracy remains competitive: HotpotQA ECE improves from 0.37 to 0.03 with accuracy changing from 63.0% to 62.1%; math ECE improves from 0.26 to 0.10 with accuracy changing from 72.9% to 72.7%.

Evaluation extends beyond the main Qwen2.5 model to OLMo-2 and Qwen3, two training domains, and multiple held-out tasks. Comparisons include expressive confidence classifiers, probes, likelihood scores, and adapted RL-calibration baselines. These provide concrete evidence supporting marginal acceptance.

The appendices strengthen the paper with dataset-level bootstrap intervals, confidence distributions, a log-score comparison, and a controlled toy example demonstrating reward collapse. Confidence-weighted voting also provides a useful downstream application.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior RL training with proper scoring rules, which the paper acknowledges. The main advance is adding a correctness term and evaluating the combination for reasoning models; uncertainty reasoning and confidence-weighted voting also have close precedents.

The theoretical presentation needs correction. Appendix A contains sign errors in the expressions for the calibration argmax and W(p), and incorrectly simplifies W'(p) to S(p,1)-S(p,0), rather than λ-S(p,1)+S(p,0). The Brier conclusion remains valid—its calibrated expected reward is p²—but the general proof requires explicit regularity assumptions. These are repairable errors, not grounds to reject the central mechanism.

The theorem establishes incentives under fixed success probabilities and ideal optimization, not a guarantee that finite-capacity models trained with GRPO become calibrated without sacrificing accuracy. The abstract's claim that the reward 'yields models' with both properties overstates this result.

The uncertainty-reasoning ablation changes prompts only at inference, so removing analysis also introduces a training–evaluation mismatch. Appendix G compares outputs from different generators. Neither cleanly isolates the causal contribution of uncertainty reasoning; matched training with and without analysis would be more convincing.

OOD improvements are uneven. For HotpotQA-trained models, CommonsenseQA ECE worsens from 0.09 with RLVR to 0.30 with RLCR, while the Brier classifier substantially outperforms RLCR on SimpleQA calibration. In math, ordinary RLCR underperforms the full classifiers on in-domain AUROC and Brier score. Broad superiority claims should reflect these exceptions.

Reproducibility and comparison controls remain incomplete: classifier training budgets and selection procedures are insufficiently specified, bootstrap intervals do not capture training-seed variation, and the Llama-3.1-8B correctness judge lacks an agreement audit. The abstention baseline is evaluated under an instruction never to abstain, which does not measure its intended reliability benefit.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of reasoning-model training with a simple, practical objective: correctness reward minus Brier loss. The central incentive argument is sound: optimizing confidence yields expected reward p², which increases with answer correctness probability p.

Calibration gains are substantial while in-domain accuracy is largely preserved. On HotpotQA, ECE improves from 0.37 to 0.03 with accuracy changing from 63.0% to 62.1%; on math, ECE improves from 0.26 to 0.10 with essentially unchanged accuracy.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: two training domains, multiple out-of-domain benchmarks, and additional OLMo-2 and Qwen3 experiments. Comparisons include full-model confidence classifiers, probes, answer probabilities, and adapted RL-calibration methods.

The appendices strengthen the contribution through calibration-only reward ablations, a concrete demonstration of log-score reward hacking, confidence-distribution analyses, and dataset-level bootstrap confidence intervals.

Confidence-weighted voting provides a useful downstream application, and the inference-time analysis ablation demonstrates that much of the calibration benefit remains available with substantially fewer generated tokens.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior RL methods using proper scoring rules and uncertainty rationales. The meaningful contribution is the joint correctness-calibration objective and its empirical validation; the underlying scoring-rule theory and confidence-weighted voting are established ideas.

The theoretical presentation needs correction. Appendix A contains sign errors in the definitions and derivations of V and W, including a final derivative that should be λ − S(p,1) + S(p,0). The general proof also uses differentiability without stating it. These issues appear repairable for the central Brier result, but the theorem establishes idealized reward incentives, not a guarantee that finite-model RL training produces accurate, calibrated models.

The uncertainty-reasoning ablation changes prompts only at inference time. Removing analysis from a model trained with it introduces distribution shift and does not isolate its training-time contribution. Appendix G also compares different generators and different input contents. Matched training runs with and without analysis would provide stronger evidence for the claimed mechanism.

Out-of-domain improvements are uneven. For HotpotQA-trained models, RLCR has worse SimpleQA Brier/ECE than the Brier classifier and worse CommonsenseQA calibration than RLVR. For math-trained models, the classifiers outperform vanilla RLCR on aggregate in-domain Brier and AUROC. Thus, broad claims of outperforming classifiers require qualification.

Reproducibility and comparison details remain incomplete: classifier/probe training configurations and data budgets are insufficiently specified, repeated RL training seeds are not reported, and bootstrap intervals capture evaluation uncertainty rather than training variability. The adapted prior-method comparisons also differ in initialization and optimization scope, complicating attribution.

The reliability and scaling claims exceed the demonstrated evidence somewhat. The Llama-3.1-8B correctness judge is not validated against human labels, and test-time voting gains are small without uncertainty estimates or matched-compute comparisons against RLVR. Better confidence estimates should also be distinguished from reducing the underlying frequency of incorrect answers.
